questions.q: What failure mode does a plain FIFO job queue produce on a cluster shared by more than a couple of researchers?
options: Jobs run faster because there's no scheduling overhead
One large sweep submitted first can block the rest of the team's jobs for a long time, regardless of importance
FIFO queues automatically balance resource usage across users
Jobs are randomly reordered to prevent any one user from dominating
questions.explain: A FIFO queue treats all jobs identically by submission order, so one person's large sweep can lock out the rest of the team until it finishes, which is exactly what scheduling policy is meant to prevent.

questions.q: What does fair-share scheduling specifically do?
options: It gives every user an identical, fixed priority regardless of usage
It lowers a user's effective priority based on how much compute they've recently consumed
It deletes jobs from users who have exceeded their quota
It splits every job evenly across all available GPUs
questions.explain: Fair-share tracks each user's recent resource usage and reduces their effective scheduling priority the more they've already consumed, which prevents one user's workload from perpetually dominating the queue.

questions.q: What happens to a running job when it is preempted by a higher-priority job?
options: It is permanently deleted and must be resubmitted manually
It is suspended or killed to free resources, then automatically requeued
It continues running unaffected, since preemption only applies to queued jobs
It is automatically given higher priority to compensate
questions.explain: Preemption suspends or kills the lower-priority running job to free up resources for the higher-priority one, and the preempted job is then automatically requeued rather than lost.

questions.q: Why do teams typically combine fair-share scoring with hard quotas rather than relying on fair-share alone?
options: Fair-share scoring is a soft nudge toward balance, while quotas put a hard ceiling that guarantees no single user exceeds a limit
Quotas are required by Slurm and cannot be disabled
Fair-share only works for CPU jobs, not GPU jobs
Quotas replace the need for a scheduler entirely
questions.explain: Fair-share adjusts priority based on usage history but doesn't impose a hard limit; quotas (per-user/team caps enforced via Slurm associations or Kubernetes ResourceQuota) guarantee a ceiling even during a priority dispute.

questions.q: Which of the following is a practical team norm the lesson recommends beyond relying on the scheduler alone?
options: Never label jobs, to keep job names short
Let early-terminated sweep trials keep running as zombie jobs to avoid interrupting them
Label jobs descriptively and kill jobs promptly once they're flagged as dead ends, rather than holding GPUs unnecessarily
Submit all jobs at the lowest possible priority to avoid conflicts
questions.explain: The lesson recommends descriptive job names (e.g. --job-name=sweep-214-trial-07) and promptly killing jobs already flagged as dead ends by early-termination policy, since zombie jobs holding GPUs waste shared capacity.
